title: 90%-Efficient Optical Storage in a Rare-Earth Crystal with a Low-Loss Impedance-Matched Cavity
authors: Weiye Sun, Fudong Wang, Mucheng Guo, Xiantong An, Zhenqi Xu, Zhehao Xu, Xingmin He, Matthew J. Sellars, Shuping Liu, and Manjin Zhong
abstract: High-efficiency optical storage in rare-earth-ion-doped crystals is challenging because of their typically weak optical absorption,which makes cavity-enhanced memories highly sensitive to parasitic intracavity loss. Here we demonstrate a 90.1(5)% storage efficiency for coherent optical pulses in an impedance-matched cavity atomic-frequency-comb memory based on Eu3+:Y2SiO5. The Brewster-angle configuration of the crystal and fully cryogenic Fabry-Pérot cavity reduce the round-trip intracavity loss to 0.37%. Quantitative modeling shows that further improvement is limited primarily by AFC preparation and its associated dispersive response rather than by residual cavity loss,identifying the principal requirements for further approaching unity efficiency.
summary: This paper reports achieving 90.1% optical storage efficiency in a rare-earth-ion-doped crystal using a specialized, low-loss, impedance-matched cavity memory. By operating at cryogenic temperatures and optimizing the cavity geometry, the researchers minimized parasitic losses. Crucially, they determined that future improvements are limited by the fundamental properties of the atomic frequency comb preparation, not by residual optical losses.
main_problem: Achieving high-efficiency optical storage in rare-earth-ion-doped crystals is challenging due to weak optical absorption and high sensitivity to parasitic intracavity loss.
main_result: The authors demonstrated a high storage efficiency of 90.1(5)% for coherent optical pulses using an impedance-matched cavity atomic-frequency-comb memory.
method: The experiment utilized a cryogenic, impedance-matched Fabry-Pérot cavity setup operating at the Brewster angle to minimize cavity losses.
model_or_system: The physical system is an atomic-frequency-comb (AFC) memory based on Eu3+:Y2SiO5 crystals. The efficiency is governed by impedance matching conditions involving cavity loss and AFC preparation parameters.
key_observables: Measured storage efficiency ($\eta$), round-trip intracavity loss ($\epsilon$), and the retrieved echo temporal profile.
important_parameters: Cryogenic temperature (3 K), low intracavity loss (0.37%), and the required impedance matching condition ($e_d \simeq 0.11$).
main_assumptions: The primary limitation to further efficiency gains is identified as the AFC preparation and its associated dispersive response, rather than residual cavity loss.
figures_summary: Figures show the setup schematic, loss dependence on angle, the retrieved echo profile demonstrating 90.1% efficiency, and simulated AFC spectra showing spectral dependence.
paper_structure: The paper presents the experimental setup and measurements, demonstrating the high efficiency achieved through loss mitigation. It then uses quantitative modeling to analyze the efficiency limits, concluding that AFC preparation imperfections are the main bottleneck.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses the practical realization of quantum memories in solid-state systems, which is a core area of research in cavity QED and quantum optics, providing crucial experimental benchmarks for theory.

Fig. 3(c) further isolates the influence of the residual optical depth dpit at the edge of the spectral pit. For dpit between 0.1 and 0.3, the storage eﬀiciency remains above 50% for input bandwidths up to approximately 17–18 MHz, and can exceed 93% for BWin < 6 MHz. As dpit increases, both the usable bandwidth and the maxi- mum storage eﬀiciency decrease. These results show that residual absorption surrounding the AFC limits both ef- ficiency and bandwidth through its associated dispersive response.
